title: Efficient Simulation of Nonreciprocal Many-body Physics via Quantum Feedback
authors: Kseniia Vodenkova, Andrew Pocklington, Fan Yang, Andrew Lingenfelter, Aashish A. Clerk, Hannes Pichler
abstract: We present a scheme to efficiently simulate nonreciprocal many-body spin models using a non-Markovian open system. Our scheme utilizes a single quantum emitter coupled to a waveguide mode that is fed back to the same emitter after a time delay. With this coherent delayed feedback, an effective nonreciprocal interaction can be engineered, wherein the emitter at earlier times affects itself at later times, creating a scalable spin chain. We show that all the steady-state quantities of such spin models can be accessed through measurement of the emitter and the output field. Furthermore, using classical feedback that resets the emitter, quench dynamics from arbitrary product states can be simulated. We demonstrate striking features of nonreciprocal models, such as the Liouvillian skin effect, anomalous relaxation dynamics, and quasi-long-range order of output photons. Finally, we show that the proposal is amenable to experimental realization and robust to imperfections. Our work establishes a feasible way to scale up a nonreciprocal many-body system, and provides a new route towards generation of exotic states of light.
summary: The authors propose using a single quantum emitter coupled to a waveguide with coherent time-delayed feedback to simulate complex, nonreciprocal many-body spin models. This method effectively creates a scalable, cascaded spin chain whose dynamics can be read out by measuring the emitter and output field. The work successfully demonstrates access to exotic nonreciprocal phenomena, proving the concept's feasibility for experimental quantum simulation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently simulating nonreciprocal many-body spin models, especially in regimes where excitations propagate unidirectionally.
main_result: They demonstrate a scalable scheme using coherent time-delayed feedback on a single quantum emitter to realize and probe nonreciprocal physics, exhibiting features like the Liouvillian skin effect.
method: The simulation maps the physical system onto an effective cascaded spin chain, allowing access to steady-state and quench dynamics via measurement of the emitter and output field.
model_or_system: The platform is a single quantum emitter coupled to a 1D waveguide mode. Nonreciprocity is engineered using coherent time-delayed feedback ($	au$), creating an effective interaction where the emitter affects itself at later times.
key_observables: Steady-state quantities, two-time correlation functions, local spin density profiles ($\langle \sigma^z_i angle_{ss}$), and output photon correlation functions.
important_parameters: The delay time $	au$, the coupling strength $\kappa$, and the loss/dissipation rates ($\gamma_L, \eta$). The maximum simulable length is limited by the ratio $\kappa/\gamma_L$.
main_assumptions: The scheme assumes the feedback delay $	au$ is large enough for steady-state access, and the reset procedure must be much faster than the interaction time scale.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical setup (QE with feedback), the mapping to cascaded spin chains, and the evolution of local observables showing signatures of nonreciprocity like the LSE.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical setup and the effective Hamiltonian, details the simulation methods for steady-state and quench dynamics, analyzes key nonreciprocal signatures (LSE, correlation decay), and concludes with experimental feasibility and limitations.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, experimentally realizable quantum optics platform (single emitter + waveguide) to study fundamental many-body physics concepts like nonreciprocity and topological effects (LSE) that are usually studied in solid-state or cold atom arrays.

(a) A single quantum emitter coupled to a 1D waveg- uide mode, subjected to coherent delayed feedback (blue lines) and incoherent measurement feedback (red lines). (b) A single quantum emitter coupled to multiple 1D waveguides, realizing up to K-local nonreciprocal couplings. (c) A single quantum emitter coupled to a 1D waveguide terminated by a Bragg mirror, mimicking a long-range interaction tail.

FIG. 2. Tensor network mapping the delayed feedback control to cascaded spin chains. (a) The full evolution corresponds to a shifted boundary condition in which the initial state of each cascaded lattice site at t = 0 is correlated with the final state at t = τ of the previous site (red tensor network connections). (b) Stroboscopic resetting can realize an arbitrary product initial many-body state.

(b)-(d) Excitation probability of spin chain sites j under incoherent pumping at the indicated times t = τ for different delay times τ.
